## Introduction

The loss of biodiversity and degradation of natural habitats are making ecosystems increasingly vulnerable to collapse. Resilient ecosystems are essential to human and planetary well-being, providing services such as clean air and water, climate regulation, nutrient cycling, crop pollination, and recreation.

An ecosystem encompasses a community of interacting species and their physical environment. Ecosystems can be classified using the [**IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology (GET)**](https://global-ecosystems.org/ "url link to the global ecosystem typology webpage"), which provides a standard framework for describing ecosystem types worldwide, and assessed using the [**IUCN Red List of Ecosystems (RLE)**](https://iucnrle.org/rle-categ-and-criteria "url link to the IUCN Red List of Ecosystems criteria"), which ranks ecosystems according to their risk of collapse. Together, the GET and RLE provide a globally consistent framework for mapping, assessing and monitoring ecosystem conservation status.

This ecosystem assessment tool is part of a wider project to develop [EcoCAT (Ecosystem Conservation Assessment Tool)](https://www.kew.org/science/our-science/projects/EcoCAT "url link to the EcoCAT webpage"){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"} as an open, flexible, and modular application to map ecosystem distribution and time-series trends, and assess ecosystem degradation and risk of collapse, following the guidelines of the IUCN Red List of Ecosystems.

## What is an ecosystem risk assessment?

An ecosystem risk assessment evaluates the likelihood that an ecosystem is at risk of collapse. The IUCN Red List of Ecosystems protocol uses information on ecosystem geographic distribution, changes in distribution over time, and the severity and extent of degradation to assess the risk of ecosystem collapse using scientifically robust and internationally recognised criteria described in the [**RLE guidelines**](https://portals.iucn.org/library/sites/library/files/documents/2024-021-En.pdf).

The IUCN RLE has been adopted as a headline indicator in the [Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF)](https://www.cbd.int/gbf "url link to the global biodiversity framework website") of the UN Convention on Biological Diversity, highlighting its importance for tracking ecosystem conservation status and supporting decision-making around the world.

## The EcoCAT project

This RLE Assessment tool is part of the [**EcoCAT (Ecosystem Conservation Assessment Tools)**](https://www.kew.org/science/our-science/projects/EcoCAT) project, a broader initiative to develop open, modular and user-friendly tools that support ecosystem mapping and assessment in line with the IUCN Red List of Ecosystems framework.

## How does this tool support ecosystem assessments?    

The **EcoCAT RLE Assessment Tool** helps users assess the risk of ecosystem collapse following the guidelines and criteria of the IUCN Red List of Ecosystems.

Users begin the assessment process by uploading ecosystem maps, which may have been generated using mapping tools or obtained from published datasets. The tool accepts ecosystem maps in GeoTIFF (.tif) raster format for a single year or multiple years (*n.b.:* maps from at least two distinct years are required to assess change over time, i.e. Criterion A). Currently, the tool assists with the following steps of the RLE assessment process:

-   **Ecosystem Description:** Document information describing the assessment unit

-   **Criterion A:** Assess risk associated with reductions in geographic distribution over time.

-   **Criterion B:** Assess risks associated with restricted geographic distribution, measured using Extent of Occurrence (EOO) and Area of Occupancy (AOO).

The tool generates outputs that support the assessment process and can be downloaded for use in reports, publications, and further analyses (see Report & Data tab):

-   Assessment report

-   Data tables

-   Spatial data

-   Publication-ready figures

## Who is this tool for?

This tool is intended for practitioners, researchers, conservationists, and decision-makers undertaking IUCN Red List of Ecosystems assessments. It is designed for users who already have ecosystem maps and wish to assess ecosystem risk of collapse following the [IUCN Red List of Ecosystem assessment guidelines](https://portals.iucn.org/library/sites/library/files/documents/2024-021-En.pdf "pdf file of the RLE ecosytem assessment guidelines"){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"}.

## Future work

Future releases of the EcoCAT RLE Assessment Tool will include support for the calculation of ecosystem degradation based on widely applicable indicators to support assessments of **Criterion C** (Environmental degradation) and **Criterion D** (Disruption of biotic processes or interactions). Additional planned developments include methods to account for uncertainties in spatial distribution and integration with the EcoCAT Mapping Tool.

The EcoCAT team is currently developing the Ecosystem Mapping Tool to support the production of ecosystem maps and time series required for the assessment and reassessment of the RLE spatial distribution criteria. These maps will include measures of mapping uncertainty and will be optimised for direct use in the RLE Assessment Tool.
